text: A second full case study — Caldwell & Finch Insurance, a fictional mid-sized insurance company, used purely as a realistic composite scenario, not based on any real company's data. This time the problem spans three separate source systems instead of one pipeline, which is exactly what makes it harder to trace than the revenue-report case.

Marketing's renewal campaign draws complaints — customers got the same email two or three times — while the customer count reported to leadership has crept up for six months despite flat growth. One cause, three systems: the CRM keys a record by CRM_ID when an agent first logs a prospect; the Policy Administration System keys a separate one by PolicyHolderID, since a policy can legally go to someone the CRM never tracked; and Support Ticketing keys yet another by email alone, with no link to either ID.

Each system's lineage is fine within itself — the problem only appears when a downstream 'unified customer view' tries to merge all three. That logic matches by email address, but the CRM and Policy Administration records sometimes store slightly different formatting for the same real person: J.Smith@email.com versus j.smith@email.com versus an old personal address never updated. So the same real customer gets counted as two or three separate rows — each with its own send-list entry, exactly why the renewal campaign fired multiple times.

Tracing upstream and downstream from the unified customer view shows it feeds four consumers: the marketing send-list export, the leadership customer-count metric, a churn-rate calculation, and a compliance mailing-address report. All four have been quietly wrong in the same direction for as long as the matching bug existed — which is why the count crept up even without real growth, as the same people slowly accumulated more duplicate variants as they updated their email in only one of the three systems.

The technical fix — standardizing email capitalization and whitespace — closes the immediate gap, but the real fix is structural: the three systems never agreed on a source of record for the customer identifier, so matching fell back on the one field all three happened to share. The lasting fix makes the CRM's CRM_ID authoritative, requires the other two systems to capture it, and documents the cross-system lineage explicitly.

Next up: a hands-on practice lab — you'll trace a lineage path through a small, fictional system yourself, on paper, no software required, using the same problem, trace, impact, fix structure from both case studies.
